prompt: how do i shade a ball so it looks round
reply:
First decide where the light comes from 💡, say top left, because every shadow follows from that one choice.
[STEPS]Leave a white dot near the light|Get darker as the ball curves away|Darkest band just before the bottom edge|Soft shadow pooling on the table[/STEPS]

prompt: how do i mix brown paint
reply:
Brown hides inside orange 🎨. Mix red and yellow for orange, then add a little blue, which dulls the orange down into brown 🟫.
Add that blue a drop at a time or you get mud. Try making three browns: chocolate, tree bark, chai.
[FACT]Blue and orange sit opposite on the colour wheel.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Mix a grey|Mix a green|Paint a sunset[/CHIPS]

prompt: why does my drawing of a road look wrong
reply:
Probably because your road stays the same width all the way up the page 🛣️. Real roads narrow: both edges lean together and meet at a single point on your eye-level line.
[STEPS]Draw a line across for the horizon|Mark one point on that line|Draw both road edges from the point|Widen them as they come towards you[/STEPS]
Look down a real street and check where the two edges seem to meet 📐.
[CHIPS]Draw a street|What about buildings|Draw railway tracks[/CHIPS]

prompt: how does a guitar make different notes
reply:
Pluck an open string and its whole length vibrates 🎸. The longer the vibrating part, the lower the note; press a fret and only the shorter piece can vibrate, so the pitch jumps up.
Try it with a rubber band over an open box: pluck, then pinch it halfway and pluck again 🎶.
[QUIZ]So a bass guitar's long thick strings give which notes?[/QUIZ]
[CHIPS]Low notes|High notes[/CHIPS]

prompt: what does 4 4 mean in music
reply:
Two numbers, two jobs 🥁. The top four means four beats in every bar; the bottom four means a quarter note gets one of those beats.
Put on a song you like and count out loud. If you keep landing on ONE at the same moment, it is in four 🎵.
[QUIZ]Using that top number, how many beats in a bar of three-four?[/QUIZ]
[CHIPS]Two|Three|Six[/CHIPS]

Carnatic music's main drum 🥁: a hollow wooden barrel with a skin head at each end, played across the lap with both hands.
The two ends are different sizes, so one hand makes deep booms and the other sharp taps. One drum, two voices, so listen for both next time 🎶.

prompt: how does one point perspective actually work
reply:
Lines running away from you appear to shrink towards a single point on the horizon, and that horizon always sits at your eye level. Widths and heights stay parallel to the page edges; only the depth lines converge.
[STEPS]Draw the horizon at eye level|Mark one vanishing point on it|Draw the front face of a box|Run each corner back to that point|Cut the box off where you want[/STEPS]
Stand in a school corridor and check whether the floor and ceiling lines really aim at your eye level 📐.
[CHIPS]Two-point perspective|Draw a corridor|Why things look faded[/CHIPS]

prompt: why do some songs get stuck in my head
reply:
Researchers call them earworms, and honestly nobody has it fully pinned down. What does show up in studies: the sticky ones tend to be simple, repetitive and slightly odd in one spot, like a leap your brain keeps replaying.
Unfinished loops seem to hang around longer, which is why deliberately playing the song right to the end sometimes clears it 🎵.

prompt: what makes a minor chord sound sad
reply:
A basic chord is three notes stacked, and the middle one decides the mood. Drop that middle note by one small step and a major chord becomes minor: same outer notes, one tiny shift, a completely different feeling 🎹.
Whether that reads as sad is partly learned, though. Listeners raised on Western music hear it strongly that way, and researchers still argue about how universal it is.
[CHIPS]Try both sounds|What is a scale|How chords stack[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i draw a portrait that actually looks like the person
reply:
Likeness lives in proportion, not detail. Perfect eyelashes on a wrong-shaped skull still will not look like them.
Measure before you render: eyes fall roughly halfway down the head, and the gap between them is about one eye wide. Then hunt the differences from that average, because their slightly wider jaw or closer-set eyes are the likeness 👤.

prompt: what is a raga
reply:
A raga is more than a scale. It is a set of notes plus rules for moving through them: which ones you use going up (arohanam), which coming down (avarohanam), which ones you lean on and ornament.
Two ragas can share the exact same notes and still be different ragas, because the movement differs 🎶.
[FACT]The seven Carnatic swaras: sa ri ga ma pa dha ni.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]What is tala|Carnatic swaras|How to listen[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do artists decide where to put things in a picture
reply:
Composition is mostly about where the eye lands first and where it travels next. One workable habit: split the frame into thirds both ways and put the important thing near a crossing point rather than dead centre, giving the subject somewhere to look or move into.
It is a starting rule, not a law, and plenty of great work is ruthlessly centred 🖼️. Crop one photo two ways and see which version holds you longer.
[CHIPS]Negative space|Try the crop test|Leading lines[/CHIPS]

prompt: why does my voice sound different in a recording
reply:
When you talk you hear yourself two ways: sound through the air, and vibration travelling through the bones of your skull. Bone conduction carries the low frequencies well, so the voice inside your head is deeper and fuller.
A recording captures only the air path. That thinner, higher voice is the one everyone else has always heard, so it is unfamiliar rather than wrong 🎤.
[CHIPS]Why singers record|How microphones work|What is pitch[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is the difference between melody and harmony
reply:
Melody is the line you would hum walking home: one note at a time, in order. Harmony is what sounds underneath at the same moment, changing how each melody note feels without changing the melody at all.
Put the same tune over different chords and it can feel triumphant or bleak, which is harmony doing the work 🎼. Hum a song you know, then listen for everything you were not humming.
[CHIPS]What is a chord|Try humming it|What is a bassline[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do painters make things look far away
reply:
Two tools, usually stacked. Perspective handles size and angle, so distant things shrink and their lines converge. Atmospheric perspective handles the rest: air scatters light, so far hills go paler, bluer and lower in contrast.
Push your background colours towards blue and save the sharpest edges and darkest darks for the front 🏔️. Check a distant hill's actual colour; it is rarely the green you expect.
[CHIPS]One-point perspective|Mix a distant blue|Paint a hill[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is konnakol
reply:
It is the spoken side of Carnatic rhythm: syllables like ta ka di mi that let you say a rhythm out loud before a drum touches it. Four syllables for a group of four, three for a group of three, and you can stack, speed up or split those groups.
Percussionists use it to learn and to teach, which is why a mridangam player often recites a phrase before playing it 🥁.
[CHIPS]Say it out loud|Try a four count|What is a mridangam[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do music producers build a beat
reply:
A common order is bottom up: kick drum first to mark the pulse, snare or clap on the backbeat, then hi-hats filling the gaps and setting the feel. Bass locks to the kick, and melody goes last, into whatever space is left.
The underrated part is subtraction, since most beats improve the moment you mute something 🎧. Tap kick and snare on a table and hear how much of a song that already is.
[CHIPS]What is a backbeat|Try tapping it|What is tempo[/CHIPS]

prompt: is it copying if i learn by drawing other people's art
reply:
Copying to learn is how nearly every artist trains: the copy is a study, and studies are legitimate. The line is what you do next. Keep it in your sketchbook, or post it and name whose work it came from; passing it off as yours is where practice stops.
Best use of a study is to copy the thing you cannot do yet, like hands or folds, not the whole picture 🎨.

prompt: why can't my hands draw what my eyes see
reply:
Mostly it is not your hands. Your brain hands you a stored symbol instead of the actual view, so ask for an eye and it supplies the generic eye icon rather than the shape in front of you.
That is why turning the reference photo upside down helps: the symbol stops firing and you draw the real lines. Plenty of people find their upside-down copy comes out noticeably better, which is annoying and useful ✏️.
[CHIPS]Try upside-down drawing|Draw negative space|Try a mirror[/CHIPS]
